old: Its oldest sense was just a box with a lid you could sit on.
In Scots it also meant a sand pit — the kind golfers still dread today.
German borrowed the coal-storage sense and gave it back to English as a bombproof shelter.
clues: This kind of protective structure began life as a humble chest whose lid doubled as a seat, with storage tucked underneath.
A hardened shelter, often underground, built to withstand bombs and attack; more heavily fortified than a cellar or foxhole. English borrowed this sense back from German during World War II.
Golfers dread landing in one, since it is also the name for a sand trap. A ship's sleeping bunk likely comes from the same old root.
